h1: Craft and mainstream beer segments for strategy teams
title: Craft and Mainstream Beer Segments | Craft Beer School
desc: A plain guide to craft, premium and mainstream beer segments for strategy teams: what separates them on the floor, in price, in channel and in the numbers.
teaser: Craft is not a small version of mainstream. It is a different business. Strategy slides rarely say why.
standfirst: Strategy teams split beer into mainstream, premium and craft. The labels sound neat. The differences underneath are about scale, ingredients, channel and cost. Here is a working guide.
sections:
Beer is beer, but the market is sliced by price and by how it is made. Mainstream beer is the volume tier: light lagers brewed at scale, often with rice or maize alongside malt, sold widely at accessible prices. Premium sits above it with higher prices and often stronger brand positioning. Craft is the smallest and most varied tier, defined by who makes the beer and how.

These tiers overlap. A brand can be premium in price and mainstream in scale. Treat them as lenses and not as boxes. A useful test is to ask which question you are answering: who makes the beer, what it costs or where it is sold. Each question draws the lines in a different place.

There is no single definition. In the United States the Brewers Association describes a craft brewer as small (up to six million barrels a year) and independent (less than a quarter owned or controlled by a drinks company that is not itself a craft brewer). It dropped an older third test, that the beer be traditional, in 2018. Other countries use different tests. India has no formal legal one.

In practice, strategy teams use craft to mean flavour-led beer from smaller, often independent producers, with many styles and shorter production runs.

Scale changes everything. A mainstream plant brews in large batches, runs packaging lines at speed and tunes recipes for consistency. A craft brewery brews many styles in small batches, uses more hops and more specialty malts and changes recipes often.

That raises cost per hectolitre and complexity. More products mean more changeovers and more small orders for ingredients. Our guide on beer production planning basics explains why variety costs more to plan. Fresh, hoppy craft beer also ages faster, so it needs a cold chain that a mainstream lager can often do without.

Craft beer is usually priced above mainstream because the cost to make it is higher and the buyer expects something different. It tends to sell through taprooms, bars, specialist retail and online where rules allow. Mainstream sells through the widest trade network.

Margin structures differ. A taproom sells directly and keeps the retail margin. A mainstream brand pays distribution and trade spend to reach every shop. Do not compare headline price. Compare contribution after the cost to reach the customer. Alcohol is a state subject in India, so channel rules differ between states. Check the current rules before you model a route.

Premiumisation means drinkers moving up to higher-priced beer. It is a trend in many markets. Craft is one of several ways it shows up. Imported brands and premium lagers capture it as well. Our guide on premiumisation in beer separates the pieces.

Do not treat craft as the whole of premium. A craft brewery in a small city is not a premium lager brand. The competitor set is different.
Reading craft share in a dashboard

A craft share figure can come from retail scans, brewery reports or surveys. Each counts different things. Retail scans miss taprooms. Brewery reports miss imports. Ask where the number came from before you build a plan on it.

Small shares can hide fast growth in a few cities and none elsewhere. Look at the city and channel cuts before you read a national line as a trend.

Ask what the segment is for. Is the aim volume, margin, brand halo or access to a new drinker? Ask what a number includes. Does craft share count only independent breweries, or any beer called craft by a large company? Ask which cost base is behind a margin claim.

Avoid market share figures from unnamed sources. Use your own sales data and trusted public reports. Our guide on the beer industry for GCC teams gives a wider frame.

Try two beers side by side: a mainstream lager and a hoppy craft ale, served cold, in small pours, with water on the table. Opt in only, within company policy, with non-drinkers welcome and spit cups for anyone who wants to taste without swallowing. Note colour, aroma and finish. That ten minutes will explain more than a slide.
faqs: There is no universal definition. In the United States the Brewers Association uses small and independent. Elsewhere the term usually means flavour-led beer from smaller, independent producers.
Is craft beer the same as premium beer?
No. Premium is a price and positioning tier. Craft describes the maker and the method. A beer can be one without the other.
Why is craft beer more expensive?
Smaller batches, more varied ingredients, more changeovers and a less efficient route to market raise cost per hectolitre.
